latin.348: & poena vocatur, quia non accidit Adamo sine divina permissione ac desertione, Deo non impediente peccati actualis naturalem efficaciam & sequelam, tum quia impediri non potuit nisi contra ordinem naturae, tum quia suo ipso peccato actuali dignus fiebat Adamus quem Deus desereret. Judicavit igitur & constituit justissime non impedire corruptionis illius productionem in Adamo. Posita autem corruptione Adami & procreatione liberorum secuta est propagatio illius corruptionis in posteros naturae vi & lege, non tamen sine Dei permissione.
latin.349: Haec permissio praeter eas rationes ob quas Deus vel Angelorum vel Adami lapsum permisit hanc habet propriam, quod necesse fuisset ad eam impediendam rescindere atque evertere leges naturalis propagationis decreto de creando mundo constitutas, quod decretum quia naturae ordine prius est decreto de permittendo lapsu, necnon decreto de reparando per Christum genere humano, non potuit nec debuit per posteriora decreta rescindi, ut iam semel monueram. Est autem decretum de non impediendo seu permittendo lapsu justum, quia nullo modo justitiae repugnat, & justum fuit ac consentaneum leges non impedire naturae: Itaque iis conservatis alia ratione hominum saluti Deus sapientissimus & optimus consulere voluit, quae naturam non everteret sed servaret. Adde quod & in ipso generationis actu & conceptione durante parentes peccant, & Deum offendunt, ut jure merito eos quatenus sanctus est deserat & naturam, quam benigne conservat, permittat, nec in eorum vel operis cui incumbunt gratiam dignetur naturae cursum impedire & leges refringere.
latin.350: Quid est in hac mea sententia quod non sit, aut Scripturae, aut rectae rationi consentaneum? Tu ipse cap. 1. constituendo statum quaestionis fassus es propagationem vitii originis fieri lege naturae, qua quisque sibi similem gignit: agnoscis igitur meae sententiae veritatem: quid est cur ea non contentus causam nostri vitii originalis Deo certo modo peccatum actuale Adami consideranti & imputanti nobis & infligenti nobis illud vitium, imputes? Dic mihi quaeso si potes, quae necessitas fuerit, cur nos omnes Deus consideraret tanquam unum hominem in Adamo? cur primum Adami peccatum actuale consideraret alio modo quam alia peccata? cur id nobis imputaret? cogeris proculdubio cum aliis quibusdam, quos nihil nominare opus est, id universum in Dei voluntatem referre.
latin.351: GAR. Primum, quae de labe seu corruptione in ipso Adamo haerente, & ex actuali ipsius peccato profecta hic dicuntur, sunt extra causam praesentem, ubi non aliud agitur, quam ut norimus, an citra imputationem peccati primi, singularis Dei judicii considerationem, idonea causa reddi possit dimanationis eius, qua corruptio moralis ex Adamo in omnes propagatur. PLAC. Nequaquam certe quae hic a me dicuntur, sunt extra causam praesentem: agitur enim etiam ut norimus, quare primum peccatum, potius quam alia peccata, corruperit naturam Adami. Id enim qui mihi in hac causa adversantur non minus Dei voluntati ascribunt, quam illius corruptionis dimanationem in posteros. Inde etiam mihi exoritur argumentum: nam si corruptio in Adamo haerens non fuit poena proprie dicta, sed secuta est necessario peccatum actuale, ut terminus ad quem sequitur motum, consentaneum est rationi, ut eadem nobis inhaerens, non sit etiam poena proprie dicta. Cur enim puniretur in nobis peccatum Adami eo malo, quo punitum non fuit in Adamo?
latin.352: GAR. Deinde ita concedit vir doctus hic intervenire justum Dei judicium, ut sua tamen justi judicii explicatione id curare videatur, ne ad communem sententiam accedat. PLAC. Id unum curo, ne quid dicam quod Dei verbo & gloriae non sit consentaneum. Non quid alii homines sentiant, sed quid sentire debeant, inquiro. Etiamsi universus mundus uno ore clamaret, cur nascamur corrupti, unicam causam esse Dei voluntatem, hoc tamen nihilominus conscientia mea refugeret, ut quod maxime. Norma fidei meae est sacra Scriptura, non opiniones hominum.
latin.353: GAR. Etenim cum docent Theologi, non esse hic simpliciter haerendum in naturali hominis propagatione, sed altius attollendos animos ad singularem voluntatem atque dispensationem Dei, & justum ipsius judicium, quid putamus justi judicii nomine ipsos intelligere; quam opus illud Dei, quo poenam aliquam ex ratione justitiae vindicatricis irrogat, quod Scriptura vocat judicium Dei contra homines Ezech. 11. 9. Quid autem vir doctus? Justum Dei judicium hic agnoscit, quia nihil fiat, nescio vel invito Deo, sed sapienter & juste permittente. Itane? Et justum judicium Dei cum Scriptura Rom. 2. 5. 2. Thess. 1. 5. Apoc. XVI. 7. XIX. 2. nihil aliud designat, quam cognitionem, sapientiam, aut permissionem Dei? Imo vero judicium Dei designat, quod vel poenas pro merito irrogat, vel praemia distribuit ex ratione justitiae illius, quae δικαιοκρισία dicitur: prout & Apoc. XIX. 2. justa Dei judicia in eo constituta dicuntur, quod meretricem illam magnam, quae corrupit terram scortatione sua, damnavit & vindicavit sanguinem servorum suorum ex manu eius.

pass_a.348: Placeus continues from the tip: Adam's corruption is called a punishment because it came with divine permission and desertion—God not blocking the actual sin's natural sequel, both because blocking it would fight nature's order and because Adam by that sin deserved desertion. God most justly judged not to hinder corruption's production in Adam. With corruption and childbearing posited, the stain spreads to posterity by nature's force and law, yet not without God's permission.
pass_a.349: That permission has its own reason beyond angelic or Adamic fall-permission: to stop the spread one would have to tear up natural-propagation laws set by the world-creating decree—prior in nature's order to permitting the fall and to repairing the race through Christ, so later decrees could not and should not rescind it. Permitting the fall does not fight justice; preserving nature's laws, God consults salvation another way that keeps nature. Add that parents sin in the very generation act, so as holy God may desert them and permit conserved nature rather than break its course for their work.
pass_a.350: What in this opinion fights Scripture or right reason? GAR himself in cap. 1 confessed original-vice propagation by nature's law of like begetting like—so he already grants Placeus's truth. Why then, not content, ascribe our original vice to God considering, imputing, and inflicting Adam's actual sin? What necessity made God treat us all as one man in Adam, treat the first actual sin unlike other sins, and impute it to us? One is forced with certain unnamed others to refer the whole to God's will.
pass_a.351: GAR says talk of Adam's inhering stain from actual sin is outside the present cause—which only asks whether moral corruption's outflow from Adam can be explained without first-sin imputation and singular judgment. Placeus: not outside at all; the cause also asks why the first sin rather than others corrupted Adam's nature, which opponents also ascribe to God's will. If Adam's inhering corruption was not properly a punishment but the necessary terminus of the motion of actual sin, then the same in us is not properly punishment either—why punish Adam's sin in us with an evil not used as punishment in Adam?
pass_a.352: GAR notes Placeus concedes just judgment intervenes yet explains it so as not to join the common opinion. Placeus cares only not to say what fights God's word and glory; he asks what men ought to think, not what they do. Even if the whole world cried that God's will alone is why we are born corrupt, his conscience would shrink from that. Sacred Scripture is his faith's norm, not men's opinions.
pass_a.353: GAR: theologians say do not stop at natural propagation—lift minds to God's singular will, dispensation, and just judgment, meaning the vindicative work that inflicts punishment from vindicative justice (Scripture's judgment of God against men, Ezek. 11:9). Placeus's 'just judgment' here is only that nothing happens without God wisely and justly permitting. But in Rom. 2:5, 2 Thess. 1:5, Rev. 16:7 and 19:2 just judgment is not mere knowledge, wisdom, or permission—it designates judgment that inflicts penalties or distributes rewards by δικαιοκρισία, as Rev. 19:2 shows in condemning the great harlot who corrupted the earth. Tip before Placeus's Scripture-locution reply.

348: And it is called a punishment, because it did not befall Adam without divine permission and desertion, God not hindering the natural efficacy and sequel of the actual sin—both because it could not be hindered except against the order of nature, and because by that very actual sin of his Adam was becoming worthy that God should desert him. He therefore judged and most justly determined not to hinder the production of that corruption in Adam. But Adam's corruption being posited and the procreation of children, there followed the propagation of that corruption into posterity by the force and law of nature, yet not without God's permission.
349: This permission, besides those reasons for which God permitted the fall of angels or of Adam, has this as its own: that to hinder it it would have been necessary to rescind and overturn the laws of natural propagation constituted by the decree of creating the world—which decree, because in the order of nature it is prior to the decree of permitting the fall, and also to the decree of repairing the human race through Christ, could not and ought not to have been rescinded by later decrees, as I have already once warned. And the decree of not hindering or of permitting the fall is just, because it in no way fights justice, and it was just and fitting not to hinder the laws of nature: and so, those being preserved, God most wise and good willed to consult men's salvation by another reason which would not overturn nature but preserve it. Add that even in the very act of generation and while conception lasts parents sin and offend God, so that as holy he deservedly deserts them and permits the nature he benignly conserves, nor deigns, for grace toward them or the work they are about, to hinder nature's course and break its laws.
350: What is there in this my opinion that is not consentaneous either to Scripture or to right reason? You yourself in cap. 1, constituting the state of the question, confessed that the propagation of original vice is done by the law of nature, by which each begets one like himself: you therefore acknowledge the truth of my opinion—what is it that, not content with that, you ascribe the cause of our original vice to God considering Adam's actual sin in a certain way and imputing it to us and inflicting that vice on us? Tell me, I ask, if you can, what necessity there was why God should consider us all as one man in Adam? why he should consider Adam's first actual sin in another way than other sins? why he should impute it to us? You will doubtless be compelled, with certain others whom there is no need to name, to refer that whole thing to God's will.
351: GAR. First, what is said here of the stain or corruption inhering in Adam himself and proceeding from his actual sin is outside the present cause, where nothing else is treated than that we may know whether, apart from imputation of the first sin and consideration of God's singular judgment, a fit cause can be given of that outflow by which moral corruption is propagated from Adam into all. PLAC. By no means certainly are the things said here by me outside the present cause: for it is also treated that we may know why the first sin, rather than other sins, corrupted Adam's nature. For those who oppose me in this cause ascribe that no less to God's will than the outflow of that corruption into posterity. From there also an argument rises for me: for if the corruption inhering in Adam was not a punishment properly so called, but followed the actual sin necessarily, as the terminus follows the motion toward which it tends, it is consentaneous to reason that the same inhering in us is not a punishment properly so called either. For why would Adam's sin be punished in us by that evil with which it was not punished in Adam?
352: GAR. Next, the learned man so concedes that God's just judgment intervenes here that nevertheless by his explanation of just judgment he seems to take care not to approach the common opinion. PLAC. This one thing I care for—that I say nothing not consentaneous to God's word and glory. I inquire not what other men think, but what they ought to think. Even if the whole world with one mouth cried that the sole cause why we are born corrupt is God's will, my conscience would nonetheless shrink from that as much as possible. The norm of my faith is sacred Scripture, not the opinions of men.
353: GAR. For when the Theologians teach that one must not simply stick here in man's natural propagation, but that minds must be lifted higher to God's singular will and dispensation and his just judgment, what do we think they understand by the name of just judgment, if not that work of God by which he inflicts some punishment from the reason of vindicative justice—which Scripture calls the judgment of God against men, Ezek. 11:9? But what of the learned man? He acknowledges God's just judgment here because nothing is done, I know not whether with God unwilling, but with God wisely and justly permitting. Is that so? And does God's just judgment, when Scripture at Rom. 2:5, 2 Thess. 1:5, Rev. 16:7, 19:2 uses it, designate nothing but God's knowledge, wisdom, or permission? On the contrary, it designates God's judgment which either inflicts penalties according to desert or distributes rewards from the reason of that justice which is called δικαιοκρισία: as also in Rev. 19:2 God's just judgments are said to be constituted in this—that he condemned that great harlot who corrupted the earth with her fornication and avenged the blood of his servants from her hand.
